content: An opsonin is any molecule that enhances the process of phagocytosis by facilitating the binding between a phagocytic cell and its target. This is often achieved by coating the negatively charged molecules on the surface of the target, thereby reducing the electrostatic repulsion between the two cells. Both the membrane of the phagocytic cell and the target cell possess a negative charge, also referred to as zeta potential. This negative charge makes it inherently difficult for the two cells to come into close proximity. Opsonization overcomes this barrier by binding antigens with specific molecules such as antibodies or components of the complement system. Phagocytic cells express specialized receptors that recognize and bind to opsonin molecules. These receptors include Fc receptors, which specifically bind to the Fc region of antibodies. When an antigen is coated with opsonin molecules, the binding of the antigen to the phagocyte is significantly enhanced. In fact, most phagocytic binding cannot occur effectively without the opsonization of the antigen. Additionally, the opsonization of an antigen and its subsequent binding to an activated phagocyte can lead to increased expression of complement receptors on neighboring phagocytes. This amplifies the immune response by recruiting additional phagocytic cells to the site of infection or inflammation. Examples of opsonin molecules include: Antibodies such as IgG and IgA. Components of the complement system, including C3b, C4b, and iC3b. Surfactant proteins. Mannose-binding lectin, which initiates the formation of C3b. Among these, the most critical opsonins are IgG and C3b, as they play a central role in facilitating efficient phagocytosis.
